variants.name: Express app.use / next() middleware stack
variants.idiom_name: app.use((req, res, next) => ...) with next() forwarding
variants.implementation_notes: In Node the pattern is the Express (and Koa/Fastify) middleware stack: `app.use` appends a function to an ordered stack and hands it the next middleware as `next`; calling `next()` forwards, writing a response or calling `next(err)` switches to error handling and stops the normal flow. Registration order is chain order, and the stack always ends in a route handler or a 404 terminal, which replaces the classic successor field. Mount paths and routers create nested sub-chains, so a middleware belongs to an explicit position in the request path.
pitfalls: Calling next() after the response was sent throws 'Cannot set headers after they are sent'; return immediately after res.send/res.json.
An async middleware whose promise rejects without try/catch and without next(err) leaves the request hanging.
Order is invisible in the route definition: a body parser registered after the route never runs, so registration stays near the top.

variants.name: Plain array-of-handlers chain (framework-free)
variants.idiom_name: const chain = [h1, h2, h3]; for (const h of chain) if (h(req) !== PASS) return h(req);
variants.implementation_notes: Without a web framework the pattern is a plain ordered array of functions, each returning either a result (it handled the request) or a sentinel meaning 'forward'. This is the form to use in browsers, workers and library code, and it is what the framework stacks are built on. The terminal case must be explicit - either a fallback step appended to the array or a checked sentinel returned by the dispatcher - because JavaScript gives no compiler help for an exhausted chain.
pitfalls: Handlers that capture mutable closure state are shared across requests; make them pure or keep per-request state on the request object.
Mutating the array while a dispatch loop iterates reorders or skips handlers; treat a chain as immutable once it is served.
Using a falsy return value as the forward signal conflates a legitimate falsy result with an unhandled request; use an explicit sentinel.
